passage: In the small town of Pilibhit, Kishore sent Ujjwal a photo from the village fair of the new swing he'd repaired, and waited in the shade of the shop. The reply came quickly: "Wow." Just that. Kishore's face fell. Ujjwal had teased him about his carpentry before, and Kishore couldn't tell if this was pride or a jibe. He walked to the roof for signal and called. "Wow, as in genuinely, wow," Ujjwal said, laughing. "You got it to swing straight!" Kishore let out a breath. Ujjwal added that he'd typed it fast from the tractor and hadn't thought how flat it would look. They agreed that next time he'd type more words.

qa.q: What did Kishore send Ujjwal a photo of?
qa.a: Kishore sent a photo of the new swing he had repaired.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he read the one-word reply?
qa.a: Kishore was unsure and a bit hurt, because he could not tell whether 'Wow' was pride or a jibe after earlier teasing. The call showed it was admiration.

qa.q: What could Kishore do next time a short reply feels unclear?
qa.a: Ask what the reply meant or call, as he did, and tell Ujjwal that short texts can sound flat.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt hearing that Kishore doubted him?
qa.a: Ujjwal was probably surprised and sorry, since he had typed fast from the tractor and meant real admiration.

grounding: A young adult reads 'wow' in a message as admiration or sarcasm, and a follow-up call clears it.

passage: Liam had finally cut off his long hair after four years. Sitting on the barber's chair in Dublin, he sent Lucia a selfie. Her reply came fast: "wow." Lowercase. Full stop. No emoji. Liam stared at it on the bus home. Was that a horrified wow? A sarcastic one? Lucia teased him about everything. He typed "that bad?" and deleted it. He typed "thanks I guess" and deleted that too. Then he just rang her. "Hi. Your 'wow' with a full stop. Good wow or bad wow?" Lucia burst out laughing. "Shocked wow! I didn't recognise you for a second. You look older. In a good way!" Liam laughed, relieved. "Next time, put a heart or something." "Next time," Lucia said, "don't make me think you've been kidnapped and replaced."

qa.q: What did Liam send Lucia from the barber's chair?
qa.a: A selfie.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when he read Lucia's "wow."?
qa.a: He felt anxious and unsure, wondering if it was horrified or sarcastic, because the lowercase word and full stop gave no tone.

qa.q: What could Liam and Lucia do to avoid this kind of mix-up?
qa.a: Add clear words or an emoji to show tone, or do what Liam did and call when a message feels unclear.

qa.q: What did Lucia actually mean by "wow."?
qa.a: Lucia was genuinely shocked and then impressed, since she didn't recognise Liam at first and thought he looked older in a good way.

grounding: Shows a young adult unsure whether a text 'wow' means admiration, shock or sarcasm, and clearing it up with a call.

passage: In the Pune boys' hostel group chat, Yusuf posted the reminder that mess fees were due by Friday, as the week's committee volunteer. Tarun, the committee head, replied within seconds: "Wow. Thanks for the news, genius 🙄". Three people reacted with laughing faces. Yusuf's ears went hot. He'd spent an hour making the list. At dinner in the mess he sat opposite Tarun. "Your 'wow' this afternoon. Was that meant the way it sounded?" Tarun started to laugh it off, then saw Yusuf's face. He put his spoon down. "Yeah. It was sarcastic. I was annoyed because I'd posted the same thing yesterday. I should've just said that." Yusuf nodded slowly. "It felt like I was being mocked in front of everyone." Tarun picked up his phone, deleted the message and typed in the group: "My bad, Yusuf's list is clearer than mine. Pay by Friday, people."

qa.q: When were the mess fees due?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when the laughing reactions came in?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, his ears going hot, because the sarcastic "wow" mocked an hour of his work in front of everyone.

qa.q: What worked in how Yusuf handled the sarcastic reply?
qa.a: He asked Tarun calmly and in person what the "wow" meant, which let Tarun admit it and fix it publicly.

qa.q: How did Tarun see his own "wow" once he saw Yusuf's face?
qa.a: He admitted it was sarcasm born of annoyance, felt he should have said so plainly, and apologised in the group.

grounding: Shows a text 'wow' that really was sarcastic causing hurt, and how asking and clear words repaired it.

passage:
Dear Tanuja,
I'm writing because my text yesterday wasn't fair to you, and a text won't fix it.
When you messaged that you couldn't come on the Goa trip after all, I replied "Wow." Just that. I know how it read. It read like "wow, typical" or "wow, thanks a lot." And honestly, in that second, some of me did mean it that way. I was disappointed. I'd booked the room.
But then Meenal told me about your mother's surgery, and I felt awful. You didn't owe me a reason, and I didn't give you room to give one.
So here's what I should have written: I'm sad you can't come, and I hope your mother is okay. I'm around if you want to talk, and the trip can wait.
Call me when you can, even for two minutes.
Sharmila

qa.q: What did Sharmila reply to Tanuja's message about not coming?
qa.a: "Wow." Just that.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when sending that "Wow."?
qa.a: Sharmila was disappointed, having booked the room, and a part of that reply was sarcastic; later, on hearing about the surgery, Sharmila felt awful.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do to repair the message?
qa.a: Sharmila wrote clearly what the reply should have said, owned the sarcasm, asked about Tanuja's mother, and invited a call.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have read the one-word "Wow."?
qa.a: Probably as "wow, typical" or "wow, thanks a lot", which would have hurt Tanuja while dealing with a mother's surgery.

grounding: Shows a young adult realising a one-word 'wow' in a text can read as sarcasm and hurt, and repairing it with clear words and an offer to call.

passage: Irawati, you want to know why I ring people now instead of typing "wow"? Okay. I'm Rehana, and last month my cousin Samira posted a photo of her new short haircut in the family group. I was on a bumpy bus and typed "wow." Just that. Wow, full stop. In my head it was a gasp: wow, you're brave, it looks amazing. Ten minutes later she messaged me privately: "if you hate it, just say so." I was stunned. I scrolled up and saw Phuppo had written "wow!!! 😍" and my cousin Adil had written "wow, bold choice." Three wows: one delighted, one maybe sarcastic, and mine, which sounded cold. So I called her from the bus stop and said, "I love it. My wow was a gasp, not a sneer." She laughed and admitted she'd cried a bit. Since then, if a wow matters, I add real words or I just call.

qa.q: What did Samira post in the family group?
qa.a: A photo of her new short haircut.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel on reading Samira's private message?
qa.a: Rehana was stunned and worried, because the plain "wow." had meant admiring surprise but had come across as cold or sarcastic.

qa.q: What did Rehana do to fix the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Rehana called Samira from the bus stop and said clearly that the haircut looked lovely and the wow was a gasp, not a sneer 😊

qa.q: What was it like for Samira reading the three wows?
qa.a: Nervous about a bold change, Samira read the bare "wow." as disapproval and felt hurt enough to cry a little.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult learning that a wow in a text can read as admiration, shock or sarcasm, and that clear words or a call prevent hurt.
